passages.t: To Timothy, my beloved child; a faith handed down
passages.happening:
Paul opens his letter in the usual way, with his name and a greeting: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus, To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord” (verses 1-2).

Then he thanks God for Timothy. He prays for him “night and day” (verse 3). “Recalling your tears, I long to see you so that I may be filled with joy” (verse 4). “I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am convinced is in you as well” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
In 1 Timothy Paul called Timothy ‘my true child in the faith’. Here he says ‘my beloved child’. Paul had helped Timothy grow in the faith for years, and he loved him like a son.

Notice the first words about life. Paul is in prison and expects to die, yet he calls himself an apostle ‘according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus’. Before he says anything about death, he speaks of life.

Then come the tears. We are not told when Timothy wept. Many readers think it was the last time they parted, perhaps when Paul was arrested. Paul remembers it, and he longs to see him again. The great apostle is not too proud to say he misses his friend.

Then Paul names two women. Timothy's father was a Greek (Acts 16:1), and it seems he did not share the faith. But his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice did. In a Jewish home children learned the Scriptures from their earliest years (3:15), and these two women taught Timothy. Their names are written into the Bible because they handed on what they believed.

Paul also says he serves God ‘as did my forefathers’ (verse 3). He did not think of his faith in Jesus as leaving Israel's God behind. He served the same God his ancestors had served, now made known in Christ.
passages.ot:
Israel's parents were told to pass on God's words at home: “And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road” (Deuteronomy 6:7). The psalms speak of the same handing on: “One generation will commend Your works to the next” (Psalm 145:4), and “We will not hide them from their children, but will declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD” (Psalm 78:4).

Paul's ‘forefathers’ recall God's name for himself at the burning bush: “The LORD, the God of your fathers—the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:15).
passages.asks: Timothy's faith came to him through a grandmother and a mother. Ask who handed the faith to you, and whether you have ever thanked them or thanked God for them. Ask to whom you are handing it on, in your family or outside it. And if no one handed it to you, notice that Paul became a father in the faith to a young man whose own father did not share it: ask who might do that for you, or for whom you might do it.

passages.t: Fan into flame the gift of God
passages.happening:
“For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands” (verse 6).

“For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The word for ‘fan into flame’ pictures coals in a fire that need stirring to burn brightly. Paul does not say Timothy's gift had gone out. He says gifts need tending. Left alone, or smothered by fear, they grow dim.

The ‘gift of God’ was whatever God had given Timothy for his work: to teach, to lead, to care for a church. Paul had once laid his hands on him, an old way of setting someone apart for a task (see also 1 Timothy 4:14, where the elders did the same).

Then Paul names the danger. It was not that Timothy lacked ability. It was fear. The word in verse 7 means timidity, the shrinking back of someone who would rather not be noticed. With Paul in chains and false teachers growing bolder, who could blame him?

But Paul says that fear is not what God gives. God gives ‘power’, strength that is not our own. He gives ‘love’, which keeps power from turning harsh. And he gives ‘self-control’, a sound and steady mind. Power without love bullies. Love without power gives up. Paul wants Timothy to have both, held steady.
passages.ot:
God gave the same word to Joshua when Moses' leadership passed to him: “Have I not commanded you to be strong and courageous? Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9). Moses too had laid his hands on Joshua at God's command: “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man with the Spirit in him, and lay your hands on him” (Numbers 27:18).

And Isaiah gave God's people the reason not to fear: “Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you” (Isaiah 41:10).
passages.hard:
Does verse 7 mean that a Christian who feels afraid or anxious has failed?

No. Paul is speaking to Timothy about courage in his work: not shrinking back from the gospel or from a friend in chains. He is not saying that anyone who feels fear has a weak faith. Paul himself admits elsewhere to sorrow and to being anxious (Philippians 2:27-28), and to the daily pressure of his care for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28). The verse points a fearful person to what God gives. It does not shame them for being afraid.

Nor is this verse a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder, panic attacks or depression. Those are real illnesses of body and mind, and they need care, not blame. Getting help is not a lack of faith, and nothing in this verse forbids it. A doctor, a counselor, medicine, one trusted person who will stay can all be part of how God cares for you. The Honest Answer ‘Is my anxiety a spiritual failure?’ says more.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul asks Timothy to tend his gift and not let fear smother it. Ask what God has given you to do, and whether fear has been keeping it small. Ask which of the three you most need today: power, love or self-control. And if you are afraid, ask who you could tell, and bring the fear to God rather than hiding it.

passages.t: Do not be ashamed: the grace revealed in Christ Jesus
passages.happening:
“So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner. Instead, join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God” (verse 8).

Paul says why. “He has saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began. And now He has revealed this grace through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel” (verses 9-10).

Paul was appointed to preach this gospel, and that is why he suffers. “For this reason, even though I suffer as I do, I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day” (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
In the Roman world, prison was a disgrace, and the shame spread to anyone who stood by a prisoner. Paul is not only asking Timothy to be brave in public. He is asking him to be seen with a man in chains, a man the empire treated as a criminal. ‘Do not be ashamed … of me, His prisoner.’ Notice that Paul does not call himself Rome's prisoner. He is the Lord's.

Then Paul packs the whole gospel into two verses. God saved us. He called us. It was not because of anything we did, but because of his own purpose and grace. And that grace was given ‘in Christ Jesus before time began’. Before the world was made, God's plan to save was already a plan in Christ.

That grace has now come into view through ‘the appearing’ of Christ Jesus, his coming into the world. And what did he do? He ‘abolished death’. The word means to make powerless, to put out of action. Death still happens. But it no longer has the last word. Christ has ‘illuminated the way to life and immortality’, turned on the light so that we can see where the road leads.

This is why Paul is not ashamed. ‘I know whom I have believed.’ Not ‘what’ but ‘whom’. His confidence rests on a person. And that person can guard what Paul has entrusted to him until ‘that day’, the day Christ returns.
passages.ot:
The prophets looked for the day when death itself would be defeated. “He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face” (Isaiah 25:8). Hosea heard God say, “I will ransom them from the power of Sheol; I will redeem them from Death. Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?” (Hosea 13:14). Paul quotes both in 1 Corinthians 15:54-55.

The psalmist trusted God beyond death: “For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (Psalm 16:10). And Daniel saw that “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life” (Daniel 12:2).

Paul's trust in the God who keeps what is given to him echoes David's prayer, which Jesus prayed on the cross: “Into Your hands I commit my spirit” (Psalm 31:5).
passages.hard:
If Christ ‘has abolished death’, why do believers still die?

Paul knew believers still died. He expected to die soon himself (4:6). ‘Abolished’ does not mean that death has been taken out of human life. It means its power has been broken. On the cross and in his rising, Christ went through death and came out the other side. So for those who belong to him, death is no longer the end, and no longer something to be ruled by fear. Paul says the same in another letter: the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:26). The victory has been won; its full result is still to come, when the dead are raised.

This is part of what all Christians confess: Jesus Christ truly died and was bodily raised from the dead, and those who belong to him will be raised too.

If you are grieving someone who has died, these verses do not ask you to stop grieving. Jesus wept at his friend's grave (John 11:35). Paul says believers grieve, but not “like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says he is not ashamed because he knows whom he has believed. Ask where you are tempted to be ashamed of the gospel, or of people linked with it who are out of favour. Ask whether your confidence rests on what you know about God or on knowing him. And ask what it would mean for you, today, that Christ has broken the power of death.

passages.t: Guard the treasure; those who left and the one who stayed
passages.happening:
“Hold on to the pattern of sound teaching you have heard from me, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. Guard the treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us” (verses 13-14).

Then Paul tells Timothy something sad. “You know that everyone in the Province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes” (verse 15).

But one man was different. “May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains. Indeed, when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me. May the Lord grant Onesiphorus His mercy on that day. You know very well how much he ministered to me in Ephesus” (verses 16-18).
passages.hearers:
‘The pattern of sound teaching’ is like an outline or a model drawing. Timothy is not to invent a new gospel. He is to keep the shape of what he was taught. But notice how he is to hold it: ‘with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus’. Right teaching held without love is not what Paul means.

‘The treasure entrusted to you’ is the gospel, handed to Timothy like money left with a trusted friend to keep safe. He cannot guard it by himself. He guards it ‘with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us’.

Then comes the hurt. The Province of Asia, with Ephesus as its leading city, was where Paul had worked for years. Now ‘everyone’ there had deserted him. Most readers think Paul means believers from Asia who could have stood by him in Rome, perhaps at his trial, and turned away. It need not mean every Christian in Asia gave up the faith. Phygelus and Hermogenes are named nowhere else. Their only memory is that they left.

Onesiphorus is remembered for the opposite. He came to Rome and searched for Paul. In a great city, with a prisoner held somewhere out of sight, that took time, effort and courage. Prisoners often depended on friends for food and clothing, so ‘refreshed me’ probably means practical help as well as company. And he was not ashamed of the chains.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament knows the pain of friends who keep away in trouble. “My beloved and friends shun my disease, and my kinsmen stand at a distance” (Psalm 38:11). “Look to my right and see; no one attends to me” (Psalm 142:4).

It also honours the friend who stays: “A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity” (Proverbs 17:17), and “there is a friend who stays closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24).

And guarding what God has given is a charge the psalms place first on God himself: “The LORD will guard you from all evil; He will preserve your soul” (Psalm 121:7).
passages.hard:
Paul prays for mercy for Onesiphorus ‘on that day’ and greets his household, not him (verses 16 and 18; 4:19). Was Onesiphorus dead, and is Paul praying for the dead?

Many readers conclude that Onesiphorus had died, perhaps after his visit to Rome. Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians have often read verse 18 as a prayer for a believer who had died, and as support for their practice of praying for the dead.

Many Protestant readers answer that the text does not say Onesiphorus had died. He may simply have been away from home, which would explain why his household is greeted on its own. They add that even if he had died, a short wish that the Lord show him mercy at the judgment is different from a settled practice of praying for the dead.

The verse is short, and we do not know what had happened. Christians have read it differently, and these notes do not choose. What is plain is Paul's thankfulness for a friend who was not ashamed of him.
passages.asks: Paul names those who left him and the one who searched for him. Ask who in your life is in a hard place that others keep away from, in hospital, in prison, out of favour, and whether you could be the one who finds them. Ask whether you hold the truth you have been taught with love. And ask who has refreshed you when you were low, and thank God for them.
